messages.mes:
*Cool wind moves through the rough grass around Alaric Red's boots.*

*The last thing that belongs to Earth is still there in memory—an old life, a world without visible mana, Classes, or this impossible second beginning. The present is different: the smell of soil and distant woodsmoke, an unfamiliar sky, and stone walls beyond the public road.*

*Alaric Red is already standing on an uncultivated roadside verge outside the nearby city. Cultivated fields and fenced holdings begin farther away. No one is close enough to have witnessed the instant of arrival.*

*The body is Human, healthy, and eighteen years old. Simple traveler's clothes are already being worn; a small pouch holding five silver rests at the belt. The memories are still from Earth.*

*A translucent interface opens across Alaric Red's vision.*

`SYSTEM INITIALIZATION COMPLETE`
`Origin: Earth`
`World: Avereth`
`Race: Human`
`Age: 18`
`Level: 1 | Rank: F`

`BASE STATS`
`STR 5 | VIT 5 | AGI 5 | INT 5 | PER 5 | WIL 5`

`Location: Public roadside verge outside Tidecross, Solmere`
`Arrival Witnesses: NONE`
`Starting Possessions: Simple Traveler's Clothes | Small Pouch | 5 Silver`
`Local Common Language: Integrated`
`Mandatory Quest: NONE`

`CHARACTER CREATION — STEP 1/2`
`Choose your Base Class:`

`Warrior   — Favored Stats: STR / VIT`
`Mage      — Favored Stats: INT / WIL`
`Guardian  — Favored Stats: VIT / WIL`
`Duelist   — Favored Stats: STR / AGI`
`Ranger    — Favored Stats: AGI / PER`

`Your chosen Class immediately applies +1 to both Favored Stats at Level 1.`
`After choosing a Class, select exactly 2 Skills from that Class's Base Skill Pool.`

`Reply with your Class choice.`

*The System waits. Story time does not move during Character Creation.*

messages.mes:
The road folded down toward the river in long, rutted curves, and Tidecross grew out of the morning haze a piece at a time: first the walls, grey stone patched with darker stone from older repairs, then the masts. They rose behind the wall like bare winter trees, dozens of them, and the smell came with the wind off the water — tar, brine, and fish.

Traffic thickened near the gate. A carter swore at his mule; two women with baskets argued cheerfully about the price of herring; a boy sprinted past with a coil of rope over his shoulder, shouting for people to make way. The gate guards barely looked up. One of them held out a hand in lazy habit, waved Alaric through with the rest, and went back to scratching his jaw at the queue of carts.

Inside, the noise hit all at once. The main street ran downhill toward the docks, cobbles worn smooth, shopfronts leaning out over the road in painted timber — a rope-walk, a cooper's yard ringing with hammer strokes, a cookhouse breathing out onion and frying fat. A merchant in a good wool coat stood arguing with a dock clerk over a ledger while stevedores wove between them with crates on their shoulders.

Alaric asked directions once, of a woman selling apples who pointed with one before going back to her haggling, and found the Guild two streets off the water: a broad stone building with a heavy door and a hanging board carved with crossed sword and staff. Inside it was cooler and quieter than the street, lit by high windows. A long counter ran along one wall, behind it a rack of pigeonholes stuffed with papers. A board stood open in the middle of the floor, sheets of parchment pinned to it in neat rows. A pair of adventurers — a broad woman with an axe slung across her back, a wiry man eating an apple — leaned at the counter talking to the clerk on duty, a grey-haired man with spectacles pushed up on his forehead.

The clerk glanced over as the door closed behind Alaric.

"Morning. Business?"

messages.mes:
The clerk counted the coins, nodded, and scratched the pen across the ledger line. "Right. Hand on the stone, then — it's just so the rolls say what you are."

He reached beneath the counter and set a grey crystal the size of a fist on the wood. Alaric rested his palm on it. For a moment the stone sat dull and dead, then a faint pulse of light moved through it from the base upward, slow as honey, and faded.

"F," the clerk said, reading the colour. "Base stage, everyone's got to start somewhere." He wrote it down without comment, then opened a shallow drawer and took out a small metal plate on a thong — stamped with the Guild's crossed sword and staff and a fresh number. He slid it across the counter.

"Guild plate. Don't lose it, it's your name in the rolls and there's a fee to replace it. Shows you're registered when you take work, turn work in, or get yourself in trouble somewhere and the local watch wants to know who you belong to."

He put the spectacles from his forehead down onto his nose and looked Alaric over properly for the first time.

"You'll be wanting the board, then. Novice work only — the postings marked for Novice rank. Anything above that and the desk'll refuse you, no offence meant, it's just the rules." He nodded toward the parchment rows standing open in the middle of the hall, where the woman with the axe was still arguing about something in low, good-humoured tones.

"Any questions about how a contract runs, ask now. Otherwise, the board's yours."

The clerk took the posting down from the board and copied its line into the ledger, then reached under the counter and brought up a flat leather satchel with a wax seal pressed over its buckle, and beside it a folded oil requisition slip.

"Gullspire Point, that's the keeper's rock, south along the coast path," he said, sliding both across. "Satchel stays sealed — the harbor warden's own wax, and nobody's business but his and the keeper's. Requisition's just paper, but the keeper needs it for his oil draw, so don't lose it in a ditch."

He stamped the slip and held it out with the contract paper.

"Active as of now. Deliver it, get nothing from the keeper but maybe a cup of something warm — payment comes back here, to the desk, sixty copper when the job's confirmed done." He glanced past Alaric's shoulder toward the door and the grey light outside. "Coast path's easy walking if the weather holds. It's maybe half a day south. 15.reply:
The south gate of Tidecross stood open, a cart of fresh fish already through it and dripping brine across the cobbles. A mason coming back the other way pointed Alaric down a lane between drying sheds, and from there the coast path found him on its own — a worn track of packed earth running above grey shingle beaches, the sea flat and dull silver to his left.

The morning passed in walking. Gulls worked the tideline. A boy with two goats and a bundle of cut gorse passed him going north and gave him the once-over, eyes settling briefly on the staff, then moved on. The satchel rode against Alaric's hip, its wax seal unbroken.

Past midday the path climbed onto low headlands, and the wind came up off the water with an edge to it that the morning hadn't had. Cloud was building out over the sea, stacked and dark underneath, and the air had the flat green smell of rain on the way.

Near the third headland the path dropped through a small cove, and there the trouble showed itself. Last night's tide, or something bigger before that, had taken a bite out of the track: a stretch of maybe ten paces where the soft cliff edge had sloughed away, leaving a steep smear of loose earth and scattered rock running down toward the water. Below the slump, the tide was already back in, waves licking at the base of the fall and leaving no strip of beach to walk around on.

Alaric stood above it and looked. The cliff material was soft, crumbly stuff. A careful crossing looked possible — the upper rim still held a narrow lip of firm ground — but a slip there would mean wet boots at best and a tumble onto rocks at worst. The other way was inland: a faint track branched up over the grass behind him, apparently cutting around the headland, adding distance and guesswork.

Out to the south, past the next point, a thin white tower stood on its rock with the first spits of rain just beginning to grey the air around it.

a faint inland track branching up over the grass that appears to cut around the headland

17.reply:
The inland track was sheep-cropped turf and old stone, climbing gently over the shoulder of the headland. The rain found it within minutes — fine at first, needling sideways, then settling into a steady drumming hiss on the grass. The track itself held firm underfoot, better than the coast path would have been, but it offered no shelter at all. By the time Alaric crested the rise, water was running off his hair and the satchel had worked around under his cloak, hugged close against his ribs to keep the wax dry.

The track bent with the land and came down through a field where a few sheep stood miserable and unbothered, then rejoined the coast path on the far side of the headland, exactly where it had promised to. The detour had cost perhaps half an hour and soaked him thoroughly into the bargain.

The lighthouse grew as he walked. It stood on a low rock stack joined to the mainland by a spit of wave-washed stone, a narrow causeway that the tide was just beginning to creep over — the keeper's rock, the clerk had called it. At its foot, half-sheltered against the tower's base, sat a squat stone cottage with smoke leaking sideways from its chimney, bent flat by the wind. A drying line strained between post and wall, and a small boat sat overturned on chocks above the tideline.

As Alaric came down the last slope toward the causeway, the cottage door opened. A broad-shouldered woman in an oilskin coat leaned out into the rain and looked straight at him, shielding her eyes with one flat hand. She watched him approach for a long moment, then called across the wind, her voice carrying clean over the water.

"Storm's coming in! If you're crossing, cross now — causeway's under by evening!"

She stayed in the doorway, waiting to see what he would do.

She jerked her thumb at the causeway — "Come on, then, before the tide makes up its mind" — and came out from the doorway, boots splashing through the first thin sheets of water washing over the lower stones. Alaric crossed the spit with the wind shoving at his back, wet rock slick underfoot, and met her at the cottage end where the ground rose dry.

She took the satchel in both hands, turned it over, and pressed a thumb against the wax seal, reading the impression the way another person might read a signature. Whatever she found there satisfied her.

"Warden Marta's wax," she said. "Good. Whole, too." She tucked it under her arm inside the oilskin and looked him over — the soaked hair, the staff, the guild plate at his belt. "Half a day's walk in this weather for a bag of letters. Sit a minute, dry off. There's a fire going."

She held out a flat palm for anything else he had. "You'll have the requisition slip too, unless they've changed how they do things. Oil draw. That one I need today — the supply boat won't run again till after the storm clears, and the lamp doesn't burn good intentions."

"That's the one." She plucked it from his fingers before the wind could, held it close under the oilskin, and read it by squint and habit despite the rain sheeting past the doorway. "Oil draw, four casks, Warden's countersign. Aye, that's the paperwork."

She tucked the slip away with the satchel, then looked up at him again, rain running off the peak of her coat between them.

"Suit yourself." She shrugged against the doorframe, unhurried. "Slip's your proof, then — Guild will want it back at the desk. Mind the causeway."

She watched him cross the spit, rain lashing the shallows that were already tongueing over the lower stones, and was gone inside before he reached the far side.

The walk back was worse than the walk out. The wind had swung with the storm and now came straight off the sea, driving the rain into his face the whole length of the coast path. By the time Tidecross walls rose out of the grey, the light had gone thin and late, drains were chuckling in the gutters, and the lamp-watch had lit the lanterns over the south gate early. Alaric came up the main street soaked to the skin, boots squelching, and pushed open the Guild hall door on a wash of warm lamplight and peat smoke.

The hall was nearly empty this close to evening — a pair of Proven-rank men drying their cloaks by the hearth, a board of postings along the far wall. The grey-haired clerk with the spectacles pushed up on his forehead sat at the front desk, copying entries into a ledger, and looked up at the drip Alaric left on his floorboards.

"Back already." He held out a hand, palm up. "Slip and word it went whole?"

Alaric gave him the requisition slip and told him the keeper had taken the satchel, wax intact, and the oil draw with it. The clerk turned the slip over, checked the countersign against something in a drawer, and made a short entry in the ledger with a pencil that had seen better years.

"Letters to the Lighthouse Keeper, closed." He counted out sixty coppers from the till, stacked them, and slid the little tower of coin across the desk. "Sixty. Done before the storm, too — half the hall wouldn't have crossed that causeway today. Anything else, or are you for a fire?"

deltas.text: The clerk noted Alaric crossed the storm-lashed causeway back before the storm, something half the hall wouldn't have done.
